title: Expander Turbine

introduction.definition: A turboexpander is a radial-inflow turbine through which high-pressure gas expands. Because the gas does work on the wheel, its temperature drops far more than across a valve (near-isentropic expansion). The power is recovered in a compressor wheel on the same shaft or a generator.
key_points: Seal gas keeps oil out of the process
introduction.summary: A turboexpander lets high-pressure gas expand through a radial-inflow turbine wheel. Because the gas does work on the wheel, its temperature drops far more than in a valve — the basis of gas processing, air separation and LNG refrigeration. The recovered power drives a compressor wheel on the same shaft (or a generator). Variable inlet guide vanes control the flow.

pressure.title: Expander: pressure and temperature drop
pressure.description: High-pressure gas enters the scroll, accelerates through the nozzles and expands through the wheel, doing work on it. Pressure and temperature fall sharply (refrigeration effect); the power drives the compressor (or a generator) on the same shaft.

foundation: Mount on a rigid, level foundation or grouted baseplate sized for the machine mass and dynamic loads (typically ≥3–5 × machine mass for reciprocating machines).
Check for soft foot before final bolting.
alignment: Align driver and driven shafts with a laser or dial-indicator method to the coupling maker's tolerances; re-check hot alignment where thermal growth is significant.
piping: Fit inlet strainers (fine screens) to protect the wheel; liquids/solids must be removed upstream.
commissioning: Check rotation direction with the coupling disconnected.
Fill lubricant to the correct level and grade.
Start unloaded where possible; record vibration, temperatures, current and pressures as a baseline.

routine.task: Monitor speed, vibration, bearing temperatures and seal-gas ΔP.

periodic.task: Clean inlet screen; check nozzle actuator.

overhaul.task: Replace bearings and seals; inspect wheels.

lubrication: Pressurised lube-oil system (or active magnetic bearings with no oil).

video_tutorials.title: Expander Turbine — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Expander Turbine.
A turboexpander is a radial-inflow turbine through which high-pressure gas expands.
Because the gas does work on the wheel, its temperature drops far more than across a valve (near-isentropic expansion).
The power is recovered in a compressor wheel on the same shaft or a generator.
Typical applications include natural-gas processing (NGL recovery, dew-point control); air separation (cryogenic); LNG and hydrogen liquefaction; pressure letdown energy recovery.

The cutaway reveals the internal construction: Rotor: Expander Wheel, Shaft & Compressor Wheel, Expander Inlet Scroll & Axial Exhaust (cold gas out), Compressor (Brake) Casing: Axial Inlet, Diffuser & Volute.
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.
Next, watch the operation tutorial to see how it works.

video_tutorials.title: Expander Turbine — Operation

script.narration: How the Expander Turbine works.
High-pressure gas enters the inlet scroll.
Variable nozzles accelerate it onto the wheel and control the flow.
The gas expands through the expander wheel, cooling strongly and driving the shaft.
The same shaft drives the compressor wheel, which recompresses gas.
Tilting-pad bearings and seals in the centre housing support the high-speed rotor.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.
High-pressure gas enters the scroll, accelerates through the nozzles and expands through the wheel, doing work on it.

video_tutorials.title: Expander Turbine — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Expander Turbine.
Monitor speed, vibration, bearing temperatures and seal-gas ΔP.
Clean inlet screen; check nozzle actuator.
Replace bearings and seals; inspect wheels.
Watch for wheel erosion: efficiency loss, vibration. Common cause: liquid droplets or solids.
Watch for oil contamination of process: oil in cold box. Common cause: seal-gas failure.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
